questions.question_text: How is $0510$ read in 24-hour time language?

options.why: Reads all four digits as one ordinary number instead of hour and minute pairs.
Joins the hour and minute values instead of reading both pairs.

questions.solution_text: $0510$ is read as **zero five ten hours**.

questions.question_text: Which part of the day contains $1425$?

options.why: Treats hour 14 as though it were before the noon boundary.
Confuses hour 14 with the zero hours immediately after midnight.

questions.solution_text:
Hour $14$ is after noon and before evening.
$1425$ is in the **afternoon**.

options.why: Chooses midnight, which begins the day, instead of noon.
Uses a nonstandard end-of-day label instead of the four-digit noon time.

questions.solution_text:
Noon is hour $12$ with zero minutes.
$1200$

options.why: Uses both an invalid hour 24 and an invalid minute value 60.
Uses 64 minutes, but the minute part can only reach 59.
Uses hour 25, but the hour part can only reach 23.

questions.solution_text:
Valid hours are $00$–$23$ and valid minutes are $00$–$59$.
$2258$ is valid.

questions.question_text: Starting late in one day, which sequence is chronological across midnight?

options.why: Orders only by the written numbers and ignores that the sequence starts before midnight.
Places 1:30 am before 12:10 am and then moves back to the previous day.

questions.solution_text:
$2345$ is before midnight, followed by $0010$ and then $0130$.
The order is $2345,0010,0130$.

options.why: Confuses hour 00 with hour 12, which represents noon.
Treats the minute value as a countdown instead of minutes after hour 00.

questions.solution_text:
Hour $00$ begins at midnight and the minute part is $07$.
$0007$ is seven minutes after midnight.
